passage:
At dusk, walking home from the fields, Vaibhav stopped dead by the old banyan tree. "Amma, there's a bhoot up there. I heard it whoosh."
Indu didn't laugh. She crouched beside him. "You heard a whoosh? That sounds scary. Shall we be detectives and look?"
They stood still. Whoosh. A dark shape swooped out of the branches.
"That's a bat," Indu said. "Bats wake up in the evening to catch insects. They're shy. They won't come to us."
Vaibhav held her hand tighter. "Detective bat-watchers?"
"Detective bat-watchers," she agreed. He counted three more bats all the way home.

qa.q: What swooped out of the banyan tree?
qa.a: A dark shape, which Indu said was a bat.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav stop dead by the tree?
qa.a: He heard a whoosh and imagined a bhoot, so he felt scared.

qa.q: Which of Indu's choices helped Vaibhav most?
qa.a: She took his fear seriously, made it a detective game, and gave a simple true explanation about bats instead of laughing or adding scary stories.

qa.q: What would change if Indu had said, 'Yes, bhoots live there, so hurry home'?
qa.a: Vaibhav would likely become more frightened of the tree and the dark, perhaps for a long time.

grounding: A village mother plays along with her son's fear of a ghost in a tree, checks it with him, and gently explains the bats.

passage:
The washing machine began its spin, rumbling like thunder in the little São Paulo apartment. Tomás, four, raced into the kitchen and hid behind his mother's legs. "Mamãe, the dragon's angry!"
Priscila knelt. "The dragon sounds loud today. Are you scared of it?"
Tomás nodded hard.
"Want to see the dragon's secret?" She lifted him up to the round window. "It's the drum spinning fast to squeeze out water. That's the roar."
Tomás watched a red sock fly past. "The dragon is eating my sock."
"The dragon gives it back," Priscila laughed. "Clean."
Later he told his aunt Jana, "It's just spinning. But I call it Dragon."

qa.q: What did Tomás see fly past in the round window?
qa.a: A red sock.

qa.q: Why did Tomás hide behind his mother's legs?
qa.a: The rumbling spin sounded like an angry dragon to him, and it frightened him.

qa.q: How did Priscila mix play with truth?
qa.a: She asked about his fear, let the dragon stay as a game, and showed him the spinning drum so he learned the real cause of the roar.

qa.q: How might Jana feel when Tomás explains the dragon?
qa.a: Charmed that he knows it's just spinning but still enjoys calling it Dragon. 😊

grounding: A mother plays along with her son's washing-machine dragon, checks his fear, and shows him the simple truth without mocking him.

passage:
In the clinic waiting room, Karthik, five, pressed against Asif's side. "Abbu, will the doctor's snake-thing hear my secrets?"
"The stethoscope? What secrets?"
"That I ate the biscuits."
Across the room a mother told her son, "Sit still or the doctor will give you ten injections." Karthik's eyes went huge.
Asif lowered his voice. "Nobody gets injections for fidgeting. The stethoscope only hears your heart going thump-thump. No secrets."
"Is it scary?"
"It's cold, like a spoon. That's all."
Karthik walked in holding Asif's finger, whispering, "Cold like a spoon."

qa.q: What did Karthik call the stethoscope?
qa.a: The doctor's snake-thing.

qa.q: What was Karthik worried the stethoscope would do?
qa.a: Hear his secrets, like eating the biscuits, so he would be found out.

qa.q: How was Asif's approach different from the other parent's?
qa.a: He gave simple true facts, that it hears heartbeats and feels cold, instead of scaring with a made-up threat about injections.

qa.q: How might the boy across the room feel after his mother's warning?
qa.a: He might become more frightened of the doctor and of injections, making the visit harder.

grounding: In a clinic, a father checks his son's imaginative fear and gives simple true explanations instead of scaring him with made-up dangers.

passage: I'm Shankar, Nakul's big brother. Last week Nakul, five, woke up screaming, "A crocodile on the wall!" There was a long bumpy shadow. Papa, Madhav, didn't laugh. He sat on Nakul's bed. "A crocodile? What's he doing?" "Opening his mouth to eat me!" "Shall we see what he's made of?" Papa switched on the lamp. The crocodile was his jacket on the hook, the zip for teeth. "Your eyes made a picture from the shadow," Papa said. "Shall we name him anyway?" Nakul named him Kuku. I don't know if he was still scared, but he fell asleep holding Papa's finger.

qa.q: What was the crocodile actually made of?
qa.a: Papa's jacket on the hook, with the zip for teeth.

qa.q: What might Nakul have been feeling when the crocodile turned into a jacket?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and a bit relieved, though maybe still uneasy, since he fell asleep holding Papa's finger.

qa.q: What did Papa do well in handling Nakul's fear?
qa.a: He asked about the crocodile without mocking, showed the simple truth with the lamp, and then let Nakul play along by naming it.

qa.q: How does Shankar see what happened?
qa.a: Shankar watched Papa calmly handle the fear, but admits not knowing whether Nakul was still scared.

grounding: An older brother watches their father play along with a young child's fear, check it, and gently give a true explanation without mocking.

passage:
Monday: Chetan, five, wouldn't go up to their Kochi terrace. "A witch lives in the water tank. She eats children." His mother, Leela, crouched down. "Thank you for telling me. We'll check together."
Thursday: Leela took him up and let him hold the torch. He knocked on the tank, trembling. She lifted the lid. "Look. Water and two pipes. It fills our taps." "No witch?" "No witch." "Can we leave her a note anyway?" "Sure." He drew a smiling witch.
Sunday: Chetan told his cousin, "It's only a water tank. The note is for fun."

qa.q: What did Chetan draw on the note?
qa.a: A smiling witch.

qa.q: How can you tell Chetan was still scared on Thursday, even with Leela beside him?
qa.a: He knocked on the tank trembling, showing he still half-believed the witch might be there.

qa.q: What made Leela's approach work over the week?
qa.a: She took his fear seriously, didn't mock him, checked it with him using a torch, gave a simple true explanation, and let him keep the fun of a note.

qa.q: How might Chetan's cousin see the water tank after hearing Chetan?
qa.a: The cousin might feel less scared too, hearing from another child that it is only a water tank and the note is just for fun.

grounding: Over a week, a mother plays along with her son's fear of a witch, checks it with him and gently gives a true explanation.
